title: Short Stuff: Bliss Point
summary: Short Stuff episode on the "bliss point," the engineered balance of sugar, salt, and fat that food scientists use to make junk food highly craveable. Covers Howard Moskowitz's 1970s market research, Michael Moss's book Salt, Sugar, Fat, natural versus engineered bliss points, protein and satiety, vanishing caloric density (popcorn, Cheetos), the Optimizing Nutrition blog's suggested ratios, and famous taste-test development stories (Prego Chunky, Cherry Vanilla Doctor Pepper, Oreo flavor releases). Includes a brief ad read and casual banter.

segments.title: Bliss point defined and origins
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the bliss point as the engineered balance of fat, sugar, and salt that makes junk food hard to stop eating. They cite added-sugar consumption figures, Michael Moss's book Salt, Sugar, Fat, and Howard Moskowitz's 1970s work identifying bliss points, plus the role of psychophysics, Prego Chunky, and natural bliss points such as protein satiety.

segments.title: Why salt, fat, and sugar work together
segments.summary: Hosts explain that salt masks other flavors, sugar acts as a preservative extending shelf life, and balancing these for maximum palatability is a juggling act. They reflect on the business mindset of engineering foods people keep eating.

segments.title: Optimizing Nutrition ratio estimates and texture
segments.summary: The Optimizing Nutrition blog, drawing on hundreds of thousands of food logs, estimated a bliss point ratio: sugar about 23.5 percent of calories, about 2.9 grams of salt per 2,000 calories, and fat about 20 to 24 percent of calories. The hosts note this is not a good diet. They also mention the chewy granola bar revolution and crunchiness.

segments.title: Vanishing caloric density and Cheetos
segments.summary: Vanishing caloric density, the melt-in-the-mouth quality that stops the brain registering calories, is described with popcorn as an example. Michael Moss called Cheetos a near-perfect bliss point snack, and the hosts discuss how hard they are to stop eating. Chips' rising prices are noted.

segments.title: Personal snack anecdotes
segments.summary: Hosts share personal snacking habits, including French onion dip and a family member who ate Flamin' Hot Cheetos and then traded them at school.

segments.title: Taste testing and product development
segments.summary: Hosts describe how companies test many variations with consumers. Prego Chunky went through 45 versions, and Cherry Vanilla Doctor Pepper went through 61 versions across 4,000 taste tests.

segments.title: Oreo flavor releases
segments.summary: Hosts discuss Oreo's frequent limited flavors, including Birthday Cake and rice crispy treats, and the company's finding that limited flavors drive press and store traffic, which also boosts sales of original Oreos.

segments.title: Closing remarks
segments.summary: Hosts note Oreo is the knockoff and Hydrox was the original, then sign off with the show credit.
